openers.calabrian-age: Around 1.8 million years ago, people were already living in the hills of Georgia, far outside Africa, and their bones are the oldest human remains known beyond that continent. Within a few hundred thousand years, Homo erectus stood at Yuanmou in southern China, on Java and beside the Sea of Galilee. At home in Africa, the australopithecines that had walked there since about 4 million years ago died out, and charred bones deep in a South African cave hint that someone was handling fire. Wolves of the genus Canis spread across Eurasia, mammoths crossed into North America, and colossal floods tore across the Channeled Scablands. This chapter follows that restless stretch of the Calabrian Age, when both the planet and the human family were on the move.

gela-038.title: Dmanisi: the oldest human bones outside Africa
gela-038.text: Five skulls from a Georgian hillside changed the map of human origins. Hominins lived at Dmanisi from about 1.8 million years ago, and their fossils are the oldest human skeletal remains known outside Africa. Fossils and tools there span 1.85 to 1.77 million years, and argon dating gives 1.81 ± 0.03 million years. Skull 5 is the first complete adult hominin skull from the Early Pleistocene. The people, classed as Homo erectus georgicus, look so much like early African Homo that all early Homo may be one species. One skull belonged to a toothless old individual. Some read it as early evidence that the group cared for its old or disabled.

gela-039.title: A magnetic flip marks the start of the Calabrian
gela-039.text: Compasses would have pointed the other way for most of the early Pleistocene. Earth's magnetic field sat in a reversed state called the Matuyama chron, broken by short spells of normal polarity. One of these, the Olduvai subchron, lasted from about 1.95 to 1.77 million years ago. The Calabrian Age begins at 1.8 million years ago, just above the top of the Olduvai layers. The same level records the extinction of Discoaster brouweri, a tiny floating alga. Geologists fixed the boundary in rock at Vrica, near Crotone in southern Italy. Before 2009 this level, then dated to 1.806 million years ago, marked the very base of the Pleistocene.

gela-040.title: The wolf event spreads Canis across Eurasia
gela-040.text: Dogs' wild ancestors had a sudden boom. Around 1.8 million years ago Canis evolution exploded across Eurasia, in what is called the wolf event. The large wolf C. falconeri appeared abruptly in Europe, and C. borjgali lived alongside the people at Dmanisi between 1.8 and 1.75 million years ago. Coyote and wolf lineages later split, about 1.5 million years ago. The first coyotes appear about 1.0 million years ago, and the first wolves about 810,000 years ago.

gela-041.title: Charred bones hint at the first use of fire
gela-041.text: Deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, beyond the reach of wildfires, lie charred bones. They have been read as human use of fire about 1.79 million years ago. Yet the cited Wonderwerk study itself dates the burning to about 1.0 million years ago, so the early date is shaky. Other claims include blackened bones at Yuanmou, China, about 1.7 million years ago, and heated red sediment at Koobi Fora, Kenya, about 1.5 million years ago. Some studies read the smaller molars of Homo erectus as a sign of cooking.

gela-042.title: Diprotodon, the largest marsupial ever
gela-042.text: Australia's biggest plant-eater carried its young in a pouch. Diprotodon was the largest marsupial that ever lived and the largest herbivore on the continent. Its earliest fossils come from the Nelson Bay Formation in New South Wales and are dated indirectly to between 1.77 million and 780,000 years old. Most specimens are far younger, under 110,000 years. The oldest fossils dated directly, from Floraville, are about 340,000 years old.

gela-044.title: Homo erectus reaches China and Java
gela-044.text: Within a geological eyeblink of leaving Africa, Homo erectus stood at the far edge of Asia. It was at Yuanmou in southern China by 1.7 million years ago and at Sangiran on Java by 1.66 million years ago. A cranium from Lantian dates to 1.63 million years ago, and stone tools in northern China's Nihewan basin to 1.7 to 1.6 million years ago. Yunxian Man in China is dated to 1.77 million years ago. Java's Mojokerto child was once put at 1.81 million years, but is now dated to at most 1.49 million. By 1.3 million years ago, Oldowan tools had reached the 40th parallel at Xiaochangliang. By 1 million years ago the species had spread across Eurasia, mostly south of the 50th parallel.

gela-045.title: The last australopithecines die out
gela-045.text: A family of upright apes that had lasted more than two million years came to an end. The australopithecines arose in East Africa around 4 million years ago and died out about 1.7 million years ago. South Africa may have been their last refuge until about 2 million years ago. Climate there was growing more volatile, and they faced competition from Homo and Paranthropus. Around 2.07 million years ago, just before Paranthropus robustus and Homo erectus arrived, Australopithecus africanus vanished from South Africa's Cradle of Humankind.

gela-046.title: Two blasts build the Valles Caldera
gela-046.text: New Mexico's Jemez Mountains hide the scar of two enormous eruptions. The first, the Toledo eruption 1.61 million years ago, laid down the Otowi member of the Bandelier Tuff, a rock made of welded volcanic ash. It produced 216 to 550 km³ of dense rock, and the larger estimate makes it a small supereruption, VEI 8. A second great eruption about 1.25 million years ago laid down the Tshirege member and formed the Valles Caldera. It is one of the best-studied resurgent calderas, craters whose floors later bulged back up.

gela-047.title: Turkana Boy, the most complete Homo erectus
gela-047.text: No Homo erectus skeleton is more complete than that of a youth who died near Lake Turkana, Kenya. Known as Turkana Boy, or KNM-WT 15000, he lived between 1.6 and 1.5 million years ago. Some authorities assign him to Homo ergaster instead. His spine holds a clue about language. It could not have supported the well-developed breathing muscles that speech needs.

gela-048.title: The first Missoula floods scour the Scablands
gela-048.text: Floods of staggering size tore across the American Northwest. The oldest Pleistocene Missoula floods swept through the Channeled Scablands sometime before 1.5 million years ago. Their age comes from calcretes, hard limy soil crusts that formed in warm interglacials between flood deposits. Magnetic dating of the layers and luminescence dating, which measures when grains last saw light, back it up.

gela-049.title: Mammoths cross into North America
gela-049.text: Mammoths had been travelers for a long time. They left Africa in the late Pliocene, about 3.6 to 3.2 million years ago. The steppe mammoth arose in East Asia around 1.7 million years ago. It crossed the Bering Land Bridge between 1.5 and 1.3 million years ago and gave rise to the Columbian mammoth. DNA from a Siberian tooth 1.1 to 1.65 million years old reveals the Krestovka lineage, probably the first mammoths to colonize the Americas. Their spread south of Alaska, about 1.4 million years ago, is often used to end the Blancan and start the Irvingtonian land-mammal age. Meanwhile gomphotheres, elephant relatives, moved into South America in the Great American Interchange.

gela-050.title: Ubeidiya: Homo erectus in the Levant
gela-050.text: Just south of the Sea of Galilee, in the Jordan Rift Valley, lies one of the earliest stops on the way out of Africa. Ubeidiya records Homo erectus about 1.5 million years ago. Its layers hold simple Oldowan tools and early Acheulean ones, the shaped hand axes, about 1.4 million years old. A hominin vertebra from the site seems to belong to a different species from the Dmanisi people.

gela-054.title: The Mesa Falls eruption at Yellowstone
gela-054.text: Yellowstone's second great cycle peaked about 1.3 million years ago. The Mesa Falls Tuff eruption threw out more than 280 km³ of material. It formed Henry's Fork Caldera inside the older Island Park Caldera. High-precision argon dating pins the eruption to 1.3001 ± 0.0006 million years ago, an unusually exact date for something so old.

gela-056.title: Hominins cross the sea to Flores
gela-056.text: Reaching the island of Flores meant crossing open sea. The ancestors of Homo floresiensis probably arrived between about 1.27 and 1 million years ago. No stone tools there are older than 1.27 million years, and the oldest found are about 1 million years old. How they crossed is unknown, but Homo erectus may have built rafts by about 840,000 to 800,000 years ago.

gela-057.title: The Mid-Pleistocene Transition stretches the ice ages
gela-057.text: The rhythm of the ice ages changed, and the swings grew wilder. Between about 1.25 and 0.7 million years ago, glacial cycles lengthened from about 41,000 years to lopsided cycles of about 100,000 years. This shift is the Mid-Pleistocene Transition. Afterwards, long cold spells built ice sheets that were thicker, higher and less slippery. Each cycle then ended in a rapid jump to a warm interglacial. Around 850,000 ± 50,000 years ago, the stretch of Earth's orbit, its eccentricity, replaced the tilt of its axis as the main pacemaker of the ice ages. What caused the change is still worked out with models. They reproduce it with two slow trends: falling carbon dioxide in the air, and glaciers gradually scraping loose rock and soil off the northern continents. The new climate reached people too. A severe glacial stage, MIS 22, brought widespread drought to Africa. It may have squeezed human ancestors into a population bottleneck about 1 million years ago.

gela-058.title: The Gregory Rift begins to pull apart
gela-058.text: East Africa is slowly tearing open. The Gregory Rift, the eastern branch of the East African Rift, began spreading about 1.2 million years ago and still widens about 3 mm a year. Its faulting followed a long burst of large shield volcanoes near the edge of the old continental core, between 5 and 1 million years ago.

gela-060.title: Paranthropus, the robust hominins, dies out
gela-060.text: Big jaws and huge molars were not enough to save them. Paranthropus, the robust hominins, died out about 1.2 million years ago. The youngest Paranthropus boisei fossil, OH 80 from Olduvai Gorge, is about 1.34 million years old, though the species may have lasted to 1 million years ago. One chronology has Australopithecus and Paranthropus making stone tools right up to their extinction, no later than 1.1 million years ago.

gela-061.title: Toba's first known caldera forms
gela-061.text: About 1.2 million years ago, a volcano on Sumatra collapsed into its own emptied magma chamber. It was the earliest known of at least four caldera-forming eruptions at Toba. The same volcano would later produce {{ref:late-032}}, one of the largest eruptions of the last few million years.

gela-059.title: Homo antecessor, the pioneer of Western Europe
gela-059.text: Butchered horse bones in southern Spain show people in Western Europe about 1.2 million years ago. Cut marks at Fuente Nueva-3 record archaic humans, probably Homo antecessor, carving up the horse Equus altidens. The name means 'pioneer man', and the species is recorded at Spain's Sierra de Atapuerca from 1.2 to 0.8 million years ago. It was once proposed as the last common ancestor of modern humans and Neanderthals. It is now seen as a side branch that split off just before them.

gela-064.title: An asteroid strikes Ghana's rainforest
gela-064.text: About 1.07 million years ago, an asteroid fell into a lush rainforest in Ghana and blasted a crater 10.5 km wide. Lake Bosumtwi, about 8 km across, now fills it. Tektites, glassy beads of melted rock thrown out by the impact, lie in neighboring Ivory Coast. Smaller microtektites turn up in deep-sea sediments west of Africa.

gela-066.title: The Kidnappers supereruption buries the North Island
gela-066.text: About 1 million years ago, New Zealand's Mangakino caldera produced one of the largest eruptions in its history. The VEI 8 Kidnappers eruption released about 2,760 km³ of material in total, including about 1,200 km³ of ignimbrite. Ignimbrite is rock laid down by a scalding avalanche of ash and gas. This sheet covers more than 45,000 km², the most widespread ignimbrite on Earth. Eruptions about 1.25 and 1.0 million years ago spread such sheets across the North Island from Auckland to Napier.

gela-067.title: Kilimanjaro's Kibo and Mawenzi cones awaken
gela-067.text: Africa's highest mountain is a volcano built in stages. Kilimanjaro, 5,895 m tall, has three cones. The oldest, Shira, had been active since 2.4 million years ago. Kibo and Mawenzi began erupting about 1 million years ago. Kibo, the largest, grew in lava phases dated from about 482,000 to 170,000 years ago. Its last activity, 200,000 to 150,000 years ago, formed the summit crater. Kilimanjaro is now a dormant stratovolcano, but fumaroles in Kibo's crater still vent gas.

gela-068.title: The Pannonian Sea finally disappears
gela-068.text: A sea in the middle of Europe slowly filled with mud and sand until it was gone. The Pannonian Sea, shallow and landlocked, had existed since about 10 million years ago. It lasted until about 1 million years ago. By then 3 to 4 km of sediment had filled the Pannonian Basin.

gela-069.title: The Jaramillo flip of Earth's magnetic field
gela-069.text: For a short spell, Earth's magnetic field swung back to normal in the middle of the reversed Matuyama chron. This Jaramillo subchron is usually dated from 990,000 to 950,000 years ago, though some studies start it at 1.07 million years ago. The causes of such brief reversals are still disputed. A proposed link to the Bosumtwi impact in Ghana has been called highly speculative and refuted.

gela-070.title: Footprints on the Norfolk shore
gela-070.text: Footprints pressed into soft sediment at Happisburgh, Norfolk, are the oldest hominin tracks known outside Africa. They were made between about 950,000 and 850,000 years ago, and flint tools lie in the same deposits. Together they are the first evidence of early humans this far north. The makers may have been Homo antecessor. The beds lie between two flips of Earth's magnetic field, the Jaramillo and the {{ref:chib-001}}.

gela-072.title: Straight-tusked Palaeoloxodon leaves Africa
gela-072.text: Elephants joined the stream of animals moving out of Africa. At the end of the Early Pleistocene, about 800,000 years ago, the elephant genus Palaeoloxodon spread out of Africa and across Eurasia.

gela-073.title: A hidden impact scatters glass across Australasia
gela-073.text: About 790,000 years ago, something large hit Earth and sprayed glass over a vast area. The tektites, beads of melted rock, lie across the enormous Australasian strewnfield. Strangely, the crater has never been found. One about 100 km wide in Indochina, perhaps under Tonlé Sap in Cambodia, has been suggested. Artifacts found with the tektites tie a Homo erectus population to the impact and its aftermath. A link to the magnetic reversal of the same era is highly speculative. The two probably just happened around the same time.

gela-074.title: Cooking fish at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov
gela-074.text: Heated fish teeth in northern Israel are the oldest likely evidence of cooking. Hominins at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov left them, with traces of fire, around 780,000 years ago. It is the oldest established site outside Africa with continuous fire. Homo erectus or Homo ergaster is claimed to have controlled fire there between 790,000 and 690,000 years ago. The people also gathered and ate 55 kinds of fruits, vegetables, seeds, nuts and tubers.

reviews.calabrian-age: The Calabrian opened with people at Dmanisi, the oldest human remains outside Africa, and within a few hundred thousand years Homo erectus had reached China, Java and the Levant. Behind them the older hominin lines thinned out: the australopithecines died out about 1.7 million years ago and Paranthropus about 1.2 million years ago. Fire runs through the chapter as a thread, from disputed charred bones at Wonderwerk Cave to cooked fish at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov. Meanwhile the climate itself changed gear in the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, as ice-age cycles stretched from about 41,000 to 100,000 years. Supereruptions in New Zealand and New Mexico, impacts in Ghana and Australasia, and flips of the magnetic field kept marking the rock as the age went by.
